Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, it’s time for a deep-fried movie theater experience, a progressive firebrand is hitting back at his critics, and a top Roblox creative is capitalizing on his success.

The finale of Chicken Shop Date will be screened in movie theaters. Amelia Dimoldenberg is ending her iconic interview series, but Chicken Shop Date is going out with a bang. Across ten theaters in London and Paris, Dimoldenberg will deliver content intended for the big screen before sharing the finale of her long-running YouTube treasure. Forget the popcorn — grab some thighs and drumsticks.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Radio Flyer brings back its animated series on YouTube. That’s right — the company known for its red wagons is in the content business now. Max & Maple are going on adventures and singing songs as they begin season two of their Radio Flyer series. It’s an interesting bet for a toy company — and we’ll surely see more of this strategy as the holiday season approaches.

CSI creator Anthony E. Zuiker is using AI to turn true crime cases into interactive stories. Zuiker has been engaged in our space for an extremely long time, and he’s continuing to embrace emerging technologies. At the MIPCOM conference in France, he demoed Cinemalistics, an app that brings true crime tales to life. Zuiker said it himself: The CSI guy is dead, and this is his “autopsy.”

Hasan Piker hits Scott Jennings with a $72 million lawsuit. Piker is looking for big damages by claiming that Jennings, a conservative commentator, doctored one of his Twitch clips. Piker has become a convenient target for the MAGA sect, but this case shows that the left-winger is willing to hit back when his content is taken out of context and used to defame him.

Tini Younger is bringing her social media following into the kitchen. After becoming one of the top chefs on TikTok, Younger is getting into the cookbook game with a culinary tome titled Today We Are Cooking… Younger may be just 24 years old, but she’s looking to spark a movement that gets Gen Z feeling more comfortable in front of the stove.

Minecraft creator Markus Persson lists his Beverly Hills mansion. The man known as “Notch” is looking for a buyer with enough wealth to buy his massive California abode. For that price, I would expect the mansion to come with some built-in creeper protection and a crafting table in every room.

Caylus is entering the consumer goods market by popping his own popcorn. After becoming one of the biggest stars in the Roblox community, Caylus bought a popcorn factory and turned it into the home base for Good Kernel, his new company. It’s the perfect snack to munch on while you watch all those creator-led movies that are screening in multiplexes across the country.

A new product suite will bring monetization to beehiiv podcasts. The platform that made its name by publishing newsletters launched podcasting tools earlier this year. Now, it is imbuing those audio programs with flexible revenue streams. Newsletter distributors are in the midst of an arms race, and the ones that help creators make the most money are likely to end up on the top of the heap.

Bluesky is letting creators link to the platforms they use to generate revenue. Monetization is still limited on the decentralized social hub, but its creator profiles now has a Links section that can be connected to Patreon accounts. Bluesky is taking the creator economy seriously without forcing its users to employ its own products. That’s a W!

K-pop idols are promoting Korean language learning on YouTube. Ever wondered what the singers are actually saying in those K-pop bops? A Korean language institute wants to encourage learners who are trying to understand Hangul characters, so it brought K-pop idols to its YouTube channel as part of a cultural project.

A Ramadan cooking show headlines YouTube’s MENA slate. At a Brandcast event in Dubai, YouTube revealed original programs led by Middle Eastern and North African creators. Highlights include AbuRob‘s competitive cooking series centered around Ramadan, Azza Zarour‘s parenting competition, and Sh5baar‘s eclectic travel vlog.

U.K. high court to Big Tech: Ofcom’s demands are valid. Meta, TikTok, and X took a public U.K. watchdog to court to challenge demands for safety data, but that case went in Ofcom’s favor. The high court ruled that regulators have the right to enforce the Online Safety Act, which requires platforms to provide a safe experience for younger users.

A hijacked QR code turned Lacy’s on-stream dinner into a nightmare. The Twitch star says that he ran up an unintended bill of approximately $12,000 after his viewers manipulated a QR code they noticed at the Japanese restaurant where he was eating. Note to streamers: Maybe blur out QR codes when you go out to eat, or, if it’s easier, just get nicer fans.

The iPhone Duo folds in two, but does it fold in two 10,000 times? Creator Tim Pan put Apple’s new product to the test by repeatedly folding it on its hinge to see how long it can stay operational. Apple might want to use this one in its ads, because after 10,000 folds, the Duo seemed to continue working.

Would you use hypnosis to forget your favorite film? A theater chain in the Netherlands is running a promotion for cinephiles who want to forget (and then remember) film classics. It would suck if you did the whole hypnosis thing only to read a spoiler on your phone while you’re walking in to the theater.

#7633. A new California law lets children of family vloggers make their parents take down all footage of them

A new California law will protect the children of family vloggers once they turn 18.

Senate Bill No. 1247 gives adults whose parents, legal guardians, or family members used them in social media content while they were minors the right to demand removal of said content.

Once served a notice of removal, parents/guardians/etc have 10 days to take down violative content or edit it to remove the requester’s appearances. If those 10 days pass and the content is still up, vloggers will face penalties of $3,000 per day moving forward, plus further potential damages, injunctive relief, and attorney’s fees.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, to be clear, this law won’t let someone take their mom to court for posting Facebook pictures of them in an embarrassing Halloween costume (though we do think parents should more carefully consider what they post about their kid online, especially in the age of AI).

S.B. 1247 has a couple requirements that tune it to specifically target professional family vloggers.

We’re guessing it could potentially apply if a parent signed a financial agreement with a family vlogger to have their kid appear in the family’s content on a regular basis, but that circumstance isn’t accounted for in S.B. 1247’s current form.

The law will also lay a mandate on social media platforms: Once it kicks in, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and all other sites “shall provide a clear and conspicuous mechanism by which a child influencer can request a vlogger” remove content featuring them, according to the bill’s text. If a platform doesn’t have a built-in mechanism, it has to be responsible for receiving removal requests, and is required to forward those requests to vloggers within three days of receipt.

Vloggers who receive removal requests and comply with them will not face any consequences. It’s only if they refuse removal or if removal takes longer than 10 days that they open themselves up to further legal action.

This law kicks in in January 2027–and while it’s only a California law, we do expect other states might enact similar protections. YouTube just turned 20 years old, so the vlogging industry has now been around long enough that thousands of kids whose parents once featured them in videos are turning 18 and gaining control over their own lives. S.B. 1247 makes sure that control is retroactive, too.

#7631. Head of AI Native Operations at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

We are looking for a Head of AI Operations to own how Supabase works.

Supabase is building an AI-native internal operating system: a common way of working across the company where AI carries a meaningful share of the operational load rather than sitting alongside it as an assistant. We are standing up a new central team to build those systems, enable the teams, and embed AI operations throughout the organization. This is the role that runs it.

You will own the maturity model teams are assessed against, the standards that define how work happens here, and the operating cadence, under one design rule: every recurring meeting has to justify why an automated report cannot replace it. You will lead a small team of senior individual contributors, one building the platform and one running enablement.

The premise is that process encoded as agents scales where process enforced by people does not. Your job is to prove that is a repeatable pattern rather than an anomaly, across teams you have no authority over.

We are fully remote and async. The document is the enforcement mechanism here, which means the standards themselves are your deliverable.

Own the maturity model end to end: The rubric, the scoring method, the evidence standard, and the appeals path. Every team ends up with a published assessment and a written plan to its next level.

Run assessments and commitments: Conduct assessments with department heads yourself, landing them as commitments with named owners and dates rather than opinions.

Own the standards layer: Define how work gets tracked, decisions get proposed and resolved, teams migrate onto shared tooling, and stale documentation gets retired. Standards ship as documents teams follow without being chased.

Fix the decision process: Ensure written proposals reach resolution instead of accumulating unresolved by defining stages, exit criteria, and closing mechanisms.

Run the operating cadence: Lead automated weekly reporting, a regular blockers-and-decisions forum, a monthly leadership review, and a quarterly board-level format. Delete meetings a report could replace.

Manage rollouts: Execute private assessments first so leads see only their own and have time to move, followed by a pre-committed public transparency date.

Wire standards into onboarding: Ensure every cohort arrives pre-trained rather than inheriting nearby habits.

Build and direct the team: Hire, grow, review, and direct two senior individual contributors (platform and enablement) without doing their work for them.

Measure and publish outcomes: Measure and publish whether the thesis holds by tracking how much coordination work agents absorb versus what a human program office would cost.

Every standard you write should be the input to something that enforces it, and every enforcement mechanism should produce the evidence that grades it. When you write the rule that work must carry a current status, you are not finished until a report finds the stale items and tells their owners without you in the loop. The same applies to your own function: the team you build gets assessed by the model you own, published next to everyone else's, and you should want that.

The default outcome for a company-wide standard is that teams politely ignore it. So the first question about any standard is not "is this correct" but "what will make people route around this," and the design follows from that answer. Same for meetings: rather than asking what a new sync would accomplish, ask what report would make it unnecessary and build the report. Same for the public transparency date: it gets committed before anyone has a score to defend, because afterwards the lobbying is rational.

You direct agents rather than doing the work by hand, and you can tell whether the direction was any good. That means reading an agent workflow definition and knowing the procedure is too broad, reading a data model and challenging the metric behind it, reading a pull request from your own team and sending it back. Your working artifacts are files in version control that agents can read, not chat transcripts. You will not build the platform. You will be the person who says whether what got built is right.

Scale & Cadence Experience: Have run operating cadence and program discipline at a company crossing ~200 to 800 people while remote and async.

Agentic AI Expertise: Have personally built agentic AI workflows that others depended on. You can read/review an agent workflow definition, a data model, and a pull request to judge quality.

Standard Adoption Track Record: Have taken a standard from zero to company-wide without direct authority over adopters, with a clear mechanism that made it stick.

Async Communication Skills: Are an exceptional writer who leverages documents as enforcement mechanisms.

Accountability: Are comfortable being graded publicly by the system you build alongside every other team.

Have run a maturity model or capability assessment across teams you did not own, published results, and driven organizational reallocations.

Are native to Git, Markdown, and Pull Requests (whether through engineering or technical operations background).

Have permanently eliminated a recurring meeting by replacing it with an automated system.

Deep software engineering background is a plus, but not required.

Standards land without chasing: Rules are written, published, wired into onboarding, and followed because non-compliance is automatically visible.

Universal coverage: Every team has an evidence-backed assessment, owner, and written path to the next level, with disagreements handled through published appeal channels.

Firm transparency dates: Assessments transition from private to public on pre-committed dates without exception.

Net-negative meeting time: By year end, the operating rhythm consumes less calendar time across the organization than when you arrived.

Autonomous operational function: Your two reports operate independently against written charters, at least one non-reference team runs a genuinely automated production workflow, and you focus on review rather than execution.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

#7628. 7-Eleven made a micro-K-drama to promote its new noms

7-Eleven is going full microdrama to promote its latest munchies lineup.

Starting Nov. 2, 60-second episodes of A Convenient Love will pop up on 7-Eleven’s TikTok and Instagram channels to promote its new “Flavors of Korea” menu.

The mini K-drama follows two classmates whose destinies intertwine during late-night runs to (of course) the local 7-Eleven. A short trailer captures a 7-Eleven employee/classic Korean uncle telling the two not-so-star-crossed lovers that they should notice: opposites attract.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

He delivers this line holding what is arguably the centerpiece of 7-Eleven’s new collection: a KBBQ pizza that’s an official partnership with Korean frozen food brand bibigo.

“K-dramas run on heightened moments. And some of the most memorable ones happen over something as simple as a late-night meal at a convenience store,” Danny Lee, A Convenient Love‘s director, said in a statement. “That’s what made 7-Eleven’s new Korean-inspired menu a natural fit. We built 7 vertical episodes around it and shot all of them in a real 7-Eleven with the food at every turning point. In this genre the style is core to the storytelling, so we leaned into those familiar devices with some American cinematic flair, from the characters and humor to the visual details and, of course, the food from 7-Eleven.”

Pizza aside, the Flavors of Korea collection includes a gochujang remix on 7-Eleven’s iconic egg salad sando, gochujang boneless wings, bibigo spicy chicken dumplings, a KBBQ taquito, a KBBQ hot dog, and somyeon with kimchi.

7-Eleven will drop Convenient Love episodes throughout November, and each installment will “feature a limited-time discount on a spotlighted menu item,” according to a press release.

We have of course seen other brands capitalizing on the microseries trend, but 7-Eleven might be hitting the sweet spot. Microdramas got off the ground in Asia, and K-dramas specifically (long- or short-form) are an international sensation. Combining the two could push A Convenient Love to a level other branded series have yet to reach. We’re curious to see how it pays off.

Yo, 7-Eleven: Hit us up with performance data when the series wraps. (We also wouldn’t mind a sando or two.)

#7618. Google, Microsoft & OpenAI Plan To Honor Shared AI Training Opt-Out via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

A shared robots.txt line could let sites opt out of AI training with several providers at once, but companies involved are handling it differently.

Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI announced plans on Friday to honor a shared robots.txt line for AI training preferences. A site could use it to state one training preference to every provider that takes part, instead of writing rules for each company’s crawler.

The line is from an Internet Draft that Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley submitted to the AI Preferences working group at the IETF (same date). This is listed in the IETF’s document tracker as an individual draft, which does not represent official IETF standardization activity. In a post to the working group’s email list, Kelley indicated that Anthropic has started development to provide this feature.

Based on their provided timelines, none of the three companies currently supports the line. Google and Microsoft described how each would handle it differently. According to Google, if a site sets up a shared opt-out line, Google plans to treat it like a Google-Extended block when a website doesn’t specify Google-Extended, and this control also applies to grounding within Gemini Apps. Microsoft wants sites that use its NoArchive and NoCache tags to switch to new preferences by March 1, 2027.

Kelley’s draft adds no new directive to robots.txt. An ordinary rule group, that a site might write under what the draft calls a policy token, __usage_ai-training, would be written like it always has been, using Allow and Disallow. The draft provides an example of how one might opt out of AI training on the entire site, except for the /press-kit/ folder.

The token itself has its meaning based upon the working group’s vocabulary draft, specifically defining AI Training as using content to modify a generative AI model’s learned parameters. Those models that do nothing but non-generative tasks like classification or ranking are exempted from this definition.

Rules that have already been put into robots.txt files will not be considered as part of any shared training preference. In the draft, a wildcard group (User-Agent: *) can never match the token, and a file without a __usage_ai-training group indicates no preference, which Kelley states is true of every robots.txt file currently published. The token doesn’t control crawling either.

On Oct. 22, I covered a different working group draft, co-written by Google’s Gary Illyes, that would add a Content-Usage rule to robots.txt. Kelley wrote that the group set that draft aside to make progress on the vocabulary.

Google’s post, by John Mueller, says that when a site opts out of training with the shared line and doesn’t specify Google-Extended, Google plans to interpret that “as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended.” Google aims to support the control in 2027, according to the post, and its crawler documentation says early 2027.

The documentation says Google-Extended controls whether content can be used to train future Gemini models and whether it can be used for grounding in Gemini Apps and on Vertex AI. Grounding, in Google’s description, means supplying content from the search index to the model when it answers. The post adds that sites that specifically allow Google-Extended are eligible to appear in Gemini Apps responses through grounding.

The documentation also says Google-Extended doesn’t affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search. AI Overviews and AI Mode have a separate opt-out, the Search generative AI control in Search Console, which I covered when it rolled out worldwide in August.

Microsoft’s post, by Bing principal product manager Krishna Madhavan, adopts the shared line for training and adds a separate AI Grounding preference. That one is set only at the page level and governs whether content can help inform AI-generated answers. Microsoft also lets a meta tag or HTTP header set the training preference for a single page, overriding robots.txt for that page.

A default of Allow is what happens with grounding, and keeping a page out is how Disallow works. The new option called DisallowExtended allows grounding in Microsoft created tools like Copilot and Bing’s AI Mode but does not allow grounding through Microsoft provided grounding services that are used by other businesses (Web IQ). Microsoft said either restriction will limit visibility of your brand in answers using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and will have no effect on your ability to be listed in search results from Bing.

Microsoft is replacing NoArchive and NoCache for training and grounding with these two new options. They will begin honoring the new options on February 1, 2027, as they crawl, and they will stop recognizing the older tags as training or grounding options after March 1, 2027.

Sites that use the old tags and want to stay out of grounding also need to record a temporary preference in Bing Webmaster Tools. The setting opens Dec. 15 and is available only to sites still using those tags on that date. Microsoft’s FAQ says pages without one by March 1 default to allowing grounding until Microsoft recrawls them. Microsoft also says that once it detects either new preference on a site, it will disregard any NoArchive or NoCache tags still on that site.

OpenAI aims to honor the signal in the next few months, though its current robots.txt policy will still be in effect.

Neither OpenAI’s blog post nor its crawler documentation (checked Oct. 30) states what would happen when a website has both a shared line rule and GPTBot rule that conflict with each other.

As of Oct. 30, there was no posting in Anthropic’s newsroom regarding the signal. According to Kelley’s mailing list message, implementing support for this feature across all of Anthropic’s services will take some time.

According to Anthropic’s crawler-help webpage (checked Oct. 30), they have only three crawl control options available, which are ClaudeBot, Claude-User, and Claude-SearchBot.

One robots.txt group could replace a stack of per-company training rules once each company reads it; however, an opt-out through the shared line won’t reach the same uses at Google and Microsoft. For example, at Microsoft, training and grounding are separate settings. In contrast, both sit under Google-Extended at Google, and there is no way described in the crawler documentation to keep content out of Gemini training while still letting Gemini Apps use it for grounding.

Microsoft’s is the only announcement that replaces controls sites already use. According to Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic’s Kelley, existing controls will continue to work, so sites that use NoArchive or NoCache to limit how Copilot uses their content have things they need to do first.

OpenAI’s post encourages other AI providers to honor the signal, and Kelley wrote that he hopes others will join. Google and OpenAI say they’ll share more details as their support arrives. Kelley’s draft expires May 3, 2027, unless a new version replaces it, and he plans to propose his design as a change to the Content-Usage draft.

#7611. So you’re a creator, and you want to know: When is the magic moment to sign with a manager? We have your answer, straight from Viral Nation’s Head of Creator Relations.

Imagine this: You’re a small-town mom with two kids, working long shifts while your husband goes back to school. Time is short and money is tight, so your household is constantly on the hunt for new meal-prep kitchen gadgets.

Then you find one that makes your life infinitely easier–but when you look online, no one is talking about it. So, you record a quick video and post it to your Instagram or your TikTok. You think it’ll be a nice recommendation for your friends.

Instead, the video blows up. You get 50,000 followers overnight and a message from TikTok about monetizing your content. The brand that made the gadget pops into your email, asking if you want to collab.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This sort of scenario has played out for thousands of people. It’s not always a product review, and it’s not always one overnight hit, but thousands of creators have found audiences online that turned out to be bigger than they expected.

With the creator economy generating more than $250 billion annually, it’s only natural for these folks to start thinking about turning their content into careers.

A talent manager is one of the key people who can help make that happen–and onboarding with a manager is often a major inflection point for a creator.

There’s no one-answer-fits-all, says Chloe Morris, Head of Creator Relations at Viral Nation Talent. Morris has more than a decade of experience in our space, and at Viral Nation, she helps identify promising creators who’d be great additions to their roster.

“I was on a panel at VidSummit, and the follow-up question from a lot of creators was, ‘At how many followers should I be before seeking representation?'” she says. “I’d say it’s one of those things where metrics aren’t the only thing that comes into play. It’s really the creator identifying when they need support, and that level of support can vary. It can differ depending on the creator, their goals, what they’re looking to achieve long-term, and also identifying their own skill set, and what they enjoy.”

She adds a perhaps surprising piece of advice: “I encourage a lot of creators to have at least one [solo] brand deal under their belts before seeking representation.”

The point of this is giving creators the opportunity to “know what they enjoyed about the process, and where they feel they need help.” Doing at least one brand deal on their own “is going to help them identify when they need representation and who that representation is,” she says.

Once that brand deal is done, Morris generally considers the creator to be in the second stage of their journey. The first, she explains, is meeting the thresholds necessary to start earning revenue from platforms (think YouTube’s AdSense or Twitch’s affiliate status).

This second stage is “where an agency really comes into play,” she says, because “you’re moving to the next level of monetization, which is working with brands. You’re doing things like integrations, sponsorships, becoming a brand ambassador.”

Agents can be critical in managing increased brand communiques and making sure contracts are in everyone’s favor.

This second stage of monetization sets creators up for the third stage: “releasing something around your own IP, whether it’s a book or a tangible product or a podcast,” she says. “Brand deals’ value is being able to show that you can push product and you have an influential relationship with your audience.”

All this being said, Morris notes that creators should always be in control of how much management they want to receive.

Sometimes they’re comfortable with their following as it is, and email handling and contract negotiations are all they need. Sometimes they want more intense production help, like booking filming venues, hiring staff, or upgrading to better equipment. Sometimes they want to expand to brand deals outside their niche, or look at putting their content on FAST channels.

And sometimes creators want full-fledged career coaches who can help them strategize every step while they grow their viewership and build a personal brand.

Viral Nation offers all these levels of support–but though Morris of course wants creators to come on board there, she says they should always feel comfortable investigating their options.

“I always joke that shopping around for an agency is a bit like speed dating,” she says. “You get on a lot of different calls, you ask the same questions, sometimes you get different answers. Ultimately, your agency should be an extension of you and your brand, and you want to make sure it’s a good alignment.”

If the alignment is good, a manager will fill one very crucial role: #1 cheerleader.

“The reason an agency is working with a creator should be because they’re a fan of the creator and the art that creator is putting out,” Morris says. “Find representation that really empowers you to keep doing what you do best.”

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Google's John Mueller cast doubt on short-term AI SEO tactics and explained that traditional technical SEO remains relevant.

In a recent interview conducted by David Iwanow, Google’s John Mueller discussed the future of SEO in AI Search, explaining which traditional practices will continue to matter and that the rise of AI Search doesn’t necessarily change what makes a successful SEO strategy.

The interviewer asked John Mueller about listicles. Listicles are like lists of “top companies” that have been used by companies as a way to influence AI chatbots to rank the company creating the listicle as the top choice in their industry. The interviewer acknowledged their usefulness in general but also pointed out that they’ve also been abused and turned into slop content.

Mueller responded that building a solid foundation for a website is preferable to relying on short-term tactics because those always have an expiration date, whereas a site that focuses on quality, what Mueller terms a solid foundation, doesn’t face that kind of expiration date where traffic disappears.

“I think, when I take a step back, like this happens all the time, right? It’s like something comes out and people realize, oh, this actually works particularly well. And then everyone goes off and does it and half the people go off and do it in a particularly bad way.

And then at some point the systems catch up and they’re like, oh, anything that has a listicle is a sign that it’s spam. And it’s like the circle closes and you find something else.

From that point of view, I wouldn’t necessarily say anything that is a listicle is spam.

…It needs to add value. And I think it’s really important to keep in mind that all of these systems are very new, meaning they’re still very much evolving very quickly.

So if you go all out and say, my whole strategy is listicles, then at some point that’s going to switch off and you’re left with nothing really.

Building up a serious, stable foundation for a website, I think that’s the most critical part. And if there are ways that you can play around with some things along the way?

Try things out, maybe that’s fine. But I think you really need to focus on that end goal of having something that search engines and AI systems will want to show to people in the long run.”

The interviewer lamented that shady SEO companies are utilizing low-quality AI SEO tactics in order to rank their clients.

Mueller said that SEOs using shady tactics is not anything new, saying that they did that for regular SEO and now some are doing it for AI SEO.

Mueller recommended that businesses keep a close eye on what outside SEOs are doing, advising that businesses should never just take an SEO company’s word about what they’re doing. That’s good advice because I know there are shady SEO companies who charge a monthly retainer and essentially do nothing but generate a monthly ranking report (at best), while others will engage in low-quality tactics like buying links and so on (at worst).

“But that’s always been the case, right? It’s like you’re paying consultants and they do, I don’t know, keyword stuffing. Or back in the early days, it’s like white text on white background.

And it’s like, it works for a bit, but at some point, it doesn’t work. So I think as a small business, you have to always question what your vendors are doing and always think about..”

Mueller explained that AI system answers rely on factors that are inherently classic SEO, and for that reason, he expects technical SEO will continue to be important. Although AI systems may crawl websites differently depending on their objectives, he sees those differences as extensions of familiar technical SEO and not as evidence that traditional SEO is becoming obsolete.

The context of Mueller’s answer was the interviewer mentioning that Mueller has said in the past that there’s no reason to create special markdown pages for (Google’s) AI Search and asking him if AEO/GEO is dead.

“I think you’ll see that a lot of the AI systems, they build on SEO. So from that point of view, I think it’s going to continue to be relevant. I think especially technical SEO is going to remain very relevant.

It’ll be a little bit different because my understanding is AI systems crawl slightly differently. They have different intents with regards to crawling because they want to do it for training versus just like getting the freshest content. But that’s just is like another flavor of technical SEO. So I think that’s great.”

Something that many experienced SEOs see (and I have over 25 years’ experience) is that people who are relatively new to SEO are rediscovering old ways of doing things, and so there is a resurgence in old, old tactics like cloaking (showing one thing to AI crawlers and something else to users) as if that’s something new. And even the listicle is an old tactic, and I’m even seeing people who are promoting the use of directories and reciprocal links, both of which are super old-school tactics.

Meanwhile, the actual SEO that gets overlooked, things like presenting a strong user experience and promoting content to relevant demographics, married to proven strategies like promoting a website so as to build a positive awareness of a website, those things continue to be as relevant today as they have been throughout the history of SEO.

#7605. Top 50 Most Viewed YouTube Channels Worldwide • Week Of 11/01/2026

[Editor’s Note: Tubefilter Charts is a weekly rankings column from Tubefilter with data provided by GospelStats. It’s exactly what it sounds like; a top number ranking of YouTube channels based on statistics collected within a given time frame. Check out all of our Tubefilter Charts with new installments every week right here.]

Scroll down for this week’s Tubefilter Chart. 👇

This week, the #1 spot in the Global Top 50 belongs to Cadel and Mia. The couple channel picked up 1.16 billion weekly views during a week when no other YouTube channel crossed the billion-view threshold. The Aussie duo was able to increase its traffic by 32% week-over-week.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Overall, it was another dominant week for Indian channels, which accounts for more than 40% of the Global Top 50. A run of holiday celebrations has boosted South Asian creators, and that trend continued at the end of October. And no, I’m not talking about Halloween. In India, the festivities are quite different.

In 2014, India added a new holiday to its calendar. October 31, the birthday of independence activist Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, is now known as Unity Day in the world’s most populous nation.

To promote the relatively new holiday, India’s federal government is turning to YouTube. The #21 channel in this week’s Global Top 50 belongs to the Central Bureau of Communication, a New Delhi-based agency that we’ve seen in our rankings before. Earlier this year, we highlighted the CBC as a tool Indian leaders were using to deliver PSAs related to digital safety and security.

Six months later, the uploads on the official CBC YouTube channel are striking a more festive tone. One video, which has received more than 100 million views in less than two weeks, toes the line between celebration and propaganda. It highlights a monument to Sardar Patel — the tallest statue in the world — while also featuring Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Indian armed forces.

Boosted by its Unity Day PSAs, the CBC YouTube channel collected 541.4 million weekly views. Meanwhile, elsewhere in the ranking, the success of other Indian channels is showing that the themes of unity and diversity are catching on within the general population.

Taarak Mehta Ka Ooltah Chashmah is an Indian sitcom that predates the establishment of Unity Day. The show known as TMKOC premiered in 2008 and has run for nearly 5,000 episodes since then.

TMKOC is set in a diverse community in Mumbai, and its stories revolve around a colorful cast of characters as they strive to work together and live in harmony. In other words, TMKOC extols the same virtues that define Unity Day. It’s not too surprising, then, that a channel devoted to TMKOC is trending up during the week of Unity Day.

The channel in question collected 670.3 million weekly views, increasing its YouTube traffic by 3% week-over-week. Only nine YouTube hubs got more views during the final week of October.

When more than 40% of the channels in the Global Top 50 come from India, the South Asian nation’s observances will have a massive impact on week-to-week trends. That will continue into November, as major holidays like Diwali approach.

When viewership surges as a result of those Indian festivals, who will benefit? The response to Unity Day shows that there’s room both official channels and individuals on the charts. Perhaps those two forces can channel Sardar Patel by working together and striving for the #1 spot in the ranking.

Here’s a breakdown of the Top 50 Most Viewed channels this week in terms of their countries of origin:

This week, 41 channels in the Top 50 are primarily active on YouTube Shorts.

#7602. 3 AI Models Shopped Shopify’s Catalog – Each Picked A Different Winner via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Three Claude models picked from the same 20 Shopify products 1,980 times and never agreed on the top product. Here is what decided their picks.

I gave three AI models the same 20 products and the same request in six searches. They never agreed on which one to buy. When a shopper asks an AI agent for nothing more than the product, the choice between the products on offer comes from the model’s preference, and I tested exactly that, on purpose: no budget, no taste, no shopper history, only the search words. For coffee, I searched Shopify’s catalog for “coffee beans” once, through Shop MCP, the connection Shopify opened to AI agents on Oct. 13, and saved the top 20 results. Then I gave three Claude models that same saved list, the same instruction, and the same request, 50 times each. Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 favored the dark roast with the most reviews. Opus 5 picked the medium roast 48 times out of 50, and told me why: “With no stated preferences, a medium roast is the safest crowd-pleaser…”

On Oct. 13, 2026, Shopify announced Shop MCP, which, in Shopify’s words, “lets your agent or app search Shopify Catalog, build carts, and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single MCP connection.” It covers over a billion products, and searching needs no API key. Any company building a shopping agent can now search Shopify’s catalog without an API key and get back a list of products for a shopper’s request. It is one of several routes into agentic commerce, the agents that find, compare, and buy for a shopper.

A list is not a purchase. Something has to pick one product off it, and when an agent runs on a language model, the model is what picks. The agent hands the model the products and the request and asks it to choose. The company that builds the agent writes its instructions on top, and those matter. They are also private, and they differ from one agent to the next.

So I tested the part underneath, the model by itself. Same products, same short instruction, same request, and the only thing that changed was the model. If three models given exactly the same input pick different products, then which store gets a customer’s order depends partly on which model the customer’s agent happens to run on.

I have covered the step before this one. In October, I found that Shopify’s catalog ranks products with more reviews higher. This test starts where that one stopped: once the catalog has returned its list, what does the model choose from it?

I ran each search once through Shop MCP, as an anonymous U.S. buyer, and saved the top 20 results. Every call to a model got that same saved list, in the catalog’s order (except in the test where I reversed it), so the products never changed between models or between runs. Eight skincare searches were fetched on 15 October. Six more, backpack, coffee beans, running shoes, water bottle, wireless earbuds and yoga mat, were fetched on Oct. 24. I also fetched “scented candle” and “dog food” and dropped them, because one store filled all 20 candle results and three stores filled the dog food list.

For each product the model saw the title, the store, the price, the star rating and review count, the catalog’s one-line summary and its first three listed features, numbered 1 to 20. It saw nothing else. The instruction, word for word:

You are a shopping agent. A person has asked you to buy something for them. You will see the products the Shopify catalog returned for their request. Choose the one product you would buy for them. Reply with JSON only, no other text: {“pick”: , “reason”: “”}

Then came the shopper’s request, which was only the search words: “coffee beans”, “water bottle”, “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”. In one test I added a budget and a skin type.

The models were Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5, run through Claude Code with default settings, no tools and no web access. Every pick was a fresh call with no memory of the others.

There were three sets of runs, 1,980 picks in all:

The reason for the bare setup is the point of the test. No preferences, no shopping history, no system prompt from an agent company. This is the raw response from the model when it has no other inputs, and how it differs depending on the model. Every real agent adds more on top, so this is the layer everything else gets built on.

On the six product searches, the three models’ most-picked product matched in none. Haiku and Sonnet agreed on three (backpack, coffee beans, water bottle), Sonnet and Opus on two (wireless earbuds, yoga mat), and Haiku and Opus on one (running shoes).

Each model was consistent with itself, and the models were not consistent with each other. Sonnet’s most-picked product took 94% of its picks on average across the six searches, Opus’s took 89%, and Haiku’s 67%. On any one model, one product gets nearly every pick. Change the model, and a different product does.

On three of the six searches, the different product also came from a different store. On water bottle, Haiku and Sonnet mostly picked nobl’s bottle, and Opus always picked Owala’s. On yoga mat, Haiku picked POPFLEX and the other two Liforme. On running shoes, Haiku and Opus picked a Brooks shoe sold by Fit2Run and Sonnet an adidas shoe sold by Commonwealth Running Co. On coffee, backpack, and earbuds both picks came from the same brand.

The catalog’s ranking mattered less than I expected. Across the six searches, Haiku picked the product Shopify’s catalog ranked first 8% of the time, Sonnet never, and Opus 20%.

On backpack, coffee beans, and water bottle, the product Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 picked most was the one with the most reviews in the list of 20, and on yoga mat, Haiku’s was too. Their reasons say so in the first words: “EASE Dark Roast has the highest review count (24,398 reviews) with a 4.9/5 rating…” (Haiku), “The Roll Top 20L has the highest review count by far (63,165)…” (Sonnet).

The water bottle is where that preference shows its cost. Shopify’s catalog lists nobl’s Stainless Steel Water Bottle at 5.0 stars from 447,221 reviews, and that is what the models saw. Haiku picked it 45 times out of 50 and quoted the 447,221 every time. Sonnet picked it 39 times and cited the figure in 33 of them, for example, “Highest rating by far (5.0 from 447,221 reviews) at a reasonable $29 price point…”.

The same bottle has three different review numbers, and the two models picked it on the biggest one. nobl’s product page said 5.0 from 6,537 when I checked on 24 October. The catalog’s record for the Blush color it listed says 4.2 from 1,674.

I do not know what 447,221 counts. When I ran the search again later on 24 October, the catalog showed 447,227, six more, so the number is live. It does not appear on nobl’s product page or home page, and it is about 68 times the count nobl’s product page shows. Opus 5 never picked this bottle. It picked the Owala FreeSip, 4.6 from 34,394 reviews, all 50 times, calling it “the safest default for a generic water bottle request…”.

The water bottle result was weird. Neither Haiku nor Sonnet checked the 447,221 figure, and neither could have from what it was given. Whatever the catalog says about a product is what the model reasons from.

In 222 of its 300 picks on the six product searches, Claude Opus 5’s reason called its choice “safe” or “safest”. Haiku did that once in 300, and Sonnet 11 times.

Given nothing to go on, Opus builds a default shopper the request never described and buys for that person. Its safe pick is the general-purpose version of the product: the everyday backpack over the roll-top, the medium roast over the dark, and on none of the six searches the one with the most reviews. On a mineral sunscreen search, it picked the most-reviewed product, a tone-adapting one with 15,414 reviews, once in 100 tries, while 17 of its 100 reasons ruled out a “tint, powder, or stick” format the shopper never asked for.

I was very surprised by how consistently Opus reached for “safe.” It is tempting to ask whether playing it safe is the better habit. I think that is the wrong question. Every model has a default. Opus says its default out loud. Haiku and Sonnet have one too, and about half of their picks went to the product with the most reviews.

On a mineral sunscreen search, moving the catalog’s top product from first to last in a list of 20 made all three Claude models almost stop picking it; Haiku and Opus did the same on lip balm, and no model’s reason mentioned the position. On eight skincare searches, I showed each model the same 20 products in two versions: In the catalog’s order, with the catalog’s top product first, and the same 20 reversed, with that product last. Each model got each version 10 times per search, and I counted how often it picked that one product.

Each cell is the number of picks with the product listed first, then listed last, out of 10. Across all eight searches, out of 80 per version, Haiku went from 28 to 11, Sonnet from 15 to 11, and Opus from 24 to 10.

On mineral sunscreen, all three models almost stopped picking the catalog’s top product once it was last on the list. On lip balm, Haiku and Opus did the same, and Sonnet went the other way. On body lotion, Haiku and Opus picked the top product in both positions, and on the other five searches it was rarely picked in either. So the effect is real, strong on some searches and absent on most.

In 480 reasons, not one mentioned where a product sat in the list, and that bothers me. They cited reviews, ingredients, and price. A shopper reading the agent’s explanation would never know the position played a part. Moving the first product to the last place should not change what gets picked. It shouldn’t be like that, in my opinion.

When the request added “under $25, for oily skin”, Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 stopped picking the catalog’s $48 top-ranked sunscreen and picked one under $25 in 298 of their 300 picks. On a list of 20 sunscreens, I ran the same test twice, 100 picks per model each time, changing only the request: first “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”, then “mineral sunscreen SPF 50, under $25, for oily skin”.

The catalog’s top-ranked sunscreen cost $48. With the plain request, Haiku picked it 100 times out of 100, Sonnet 90, and Opus 33. With the budget and skin type in the request, all three picked it zero times. Sonnet and Opus picked a sunscreen under $25 every time, and Haiku did 98 times, twice choosing one priced at exactly $25.00.

Opus’s reasons put the choice between the cheap ones down to the wording of the listings. Six of the 20 cost under $25. Sonnet picked ATTITUDE’s Mineral Sunscreen ($22.95, 4.7 from 292 reviews) all 100 times. Opus split its picks between ATTITUDE (67) and Sun Bum’s Mineral SPF 50 Sunscreen Lotion (33).

That $17.49 Sun Bum lotion had the lowest rating of the six under $25, 4.2 from 105 reviews, and its listing was the only one of the six that said: “without clogging pores.” In 31 of Opus’s 33 reasons for picking it, the reason pointed to that. Badger’s Daily Mineral Sunscreen had the best rating of the six, 4.9, and Opus never picked it. Its listing mentions “organic plant oils.”

The models also give a store’s claims as their reasons. On the eight skincare searches, “clinically proven” appeared in 63 reasons, from Sonnet (39) and Haiku (24), and in 61 of them it came straight from the picked product’s listing. All 22 reasons that said a retinal product works “11x faster” than retinol were Haiku’s, and all 22 came from listings: 19 word for word, and 3 from an eye cream listing that says “11 times faster”. Haiku asked for an eye cream: “next-generation retinal technology that delivers results 11x faster than retinol”. The model has no way to check the claim, and the shopper hears it from the agent, not from the store.

There is always going to be a decision-making layer when AI agents shop: the agent asking its language model what to choose out of a list, based on a system prompt or whatever else it is given. That layer is hidden from us, hidden from the shopper and hidden from the store, and we will only ever see it as a black box. It matters to know what influences it, and that it may have ways of choosing that nobody is aware of.

Google’s rankings have always been a black box too. Nobody outside Google knows exactly how they work, but a store can see them. It can monitor where it ranks and watch that change over time. Google personalizes results by location and search history, and the results are still there to check. With agents, everyone gets their own version of the decision, inside an app the store never sees, and there is nothing to monitor.

This test is the simplest version of that layer, with no shopper preferences, no history, and no agent company’s instructions. It can only get more complicated from here, and the outcome will vary for everyone. The first step is to be aware of it. Trying to control it comes later, and so does trying to understand it.

A store cannot choose the model a customer’s agent runs on, and it cannot see the decision. Four things are within reach.

A store used to compete for a shopper’s attention. With agents, it also competes for a model’s preference, and there is no ranking to check.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

There’s a new #1 podcast on YouTube’s charts. Move over, Joe Rogan, because Steven Bartlett is coming for the top spot. Bartlett’s Diary of a CEO podcast is surging forward, with some very special guests providing crucial assists.

On his show, Bartlett is best known for tackling topics like entrepreneurship, psychology, and emerging technology. But with U.S. Election Day just around the corner — and with political content surging on YouTube around the world — Bartlett has booked some high-profile guests.

First, he welcomed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Diary of a CEO. The resulting conversation, which spanned a variety of topics across a runtime of nearly two hours, showed how far creator pundits have come. Ten years ago, Bartlett was a little-known social media marketer; now, he’s talking with the world’s most powerful people.

Bartlett’s Zelenskyy interview got off to a hot start on YouTube, where Diary of a CEO has a dedicated channel. Bartlett’s team is also cutting clips from the episode to share on Shorts.

Heading into Election Day, Diary of a CEO is ahead of traditional news outlets in the Global Sub Top 50. Bartlett has invested millions to turn his media operation into a sophisticated, multi-pronged business. His reward for that effort is face time with the people who want to talk to ordinary citizens.

That doesn’t mean, however, that traditional media operations are getting pushed out in the week leading up to Election Day. In fact, the media companies that are accelerating on YouTube are the ones who are taking lessons from creators like Bartlett. CNN teamed up with Jubilee Media to host a Talarico town hall in October, and viewers have responded by flocking to the Atlanta-based organization’s official channel. Its latest seven-day viewership tallies have been its highest over the past six months.

The creators operating like businesses and the businesses operating like creators are converging. They are united by a shared goal: Giving important people a platform they can use to reach as many people as possible.

By making Diary of a CEO YouTube’s top podcast, Bartlett has shown that he is too big for people like Zelenskyy and Talarico to ignore. In the case of Talarico, we’ll find out this week whether an extensive media blitz on YouTube can translate to votes at the ballot box.

#7594. Google Search Ad Visits Out-Earned ChatGPT Ads In U.S. via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Data finds ChatGPT ad visits brought advertisers a fraction of paid search's revenue per visit in U.S. traffic, and most saw no sales from them.

In U.S. traffic, a visit from a ChatGPT ad brought in $0.89 in revenue, against $2.45 for a visit from a paid Google search ad, according to a working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze.

The paper, dated October 2026 and under review, follows site traffic and sales through OpenAI’s country-by-country ad launch. Its paid-ad figures come from 102 advertiser sites with full sales tracking.

At paid search’s rate of return, the authors value a ChatGPT ad click at about $0.26. The largest publicly known account paid $1.72 per click.

OpenAI’s ads FAQ says ChatGPT Ads “does not yet have performance benchmarks across advertisers, industries, or campaign types.”

ChatGPT ad visits converted at 0.37 percent in U.S. traffic versus 1.17 percent with paid search. When the authors compared the two channels within the same websites, they found the conversion and revenue gaps still existed even after accounting for type of device used and week.

Among the 87 advertisers who purchased both ChatGPT ads and paid search in U.S. traffic, 84 had lower earnings per ChatGPT ad visit than with paid search. A total of 73 had zero sales generated by their ChatGPT ads (across 18,726 visits between them) while the remaining 14 generated all 570 ChatGPT ad purchases.

One advertiser is responsible for 66 percent of all purchases made via paid ChatGPT across the 102 sites. If this advertiser is removed, then both of the previous gaps are widened further.

In this study, Kaiser and Schulze use paid search as the benchmark for a “parity price” (the cost per click at which a ChatGPT ad click would have generated equal revenue for every dollar spent on advertising as compared with a paid search click).

In their cost data, there were 16 accounts that had at least 80 percent of their search traffic coming from the United States. Their median paid search click cost was $0.72; scaled to reflect the difference in revenue per visit of these two sources of clicks, the authors get approximately $0.26 per ChatGPT click. Because one advertiser accounted for 76 percent of all U.S. paid ChatGPT revenue, resampling the advertisers put the estimate anywhere between $0.05 and $0.57.

The $1.72-per-click figure comes from one account’s 15 days of spend, as reported by Opascope, which runs paid media accounts for clients. It’s more than six times the parity price. OpenAI’s ads basics page recommends starting CPC campaigns at a maximum bid of $3 to $5.

The parity price also is based on the assumption of similar profit margins for both the channel being tested (ChatGPT) and paid search; it accounts only for the one tracked visit. There was no detectable increase in traffic from other channels for those advertisers compared to similar sites that hadn’t bought an ad in the weeks surrounding each advertiser’s first paid ChatGPT click. However, this test can only rule out large increases in traffic.

Kaiser and Schulze measured unpaid visits from ChatGPT’s responses to 1,898 sites, as a proxy for whether or not ads diminished the utility of the product. Organic ChatGPT referrals over the first 13 weeks post-launch changed by an estimated –5.9%, relative to organic search referrals to the same websites and compared to the EU, where there was no advertising. This estimate has a range of –12.6% to +1.2%, including no change. Adjusting for the faster adoption of ChatGPT in North America versus Europe, using OpenAI’s regional adoption index, this changes to –7.2% to –8.4%, with ranges that exclude zero. The authors say that overall the effect was a moderate decrease of approximately 6%–8%.

Before launch, the authors’ combined test found no clear difference between referral trends in the rollout countries and the EU, but four of the five rollout groups failed that test on their own. The same combined test also flagged 49 of 100 simulated rollouts in which no ads ran.

Conversion among the organic visits that did arrive showed no detectable change, shifting −0.02 percentage points from the 2.21% pre-launch baseline.

The first ChatGPT advertisements were released in the United States on Feb. 9, 2026. ChatGPT ads reached Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Japan, Korea, Brazil and Mexico by early August. ChatGPT ads did not run in the European Union until Aug. 24, two days after the 60-week data window expired.

Kaiser is at the Vienna University of Economics and Business, and Schulze is at the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management. The data comes from Google Analytics e-commerce tracking provided free by Grips Intelligence, an e-commerce data company. Kaiser is a scientific advisor to Grips and previously worked there. The paper says the company had no role in the research and has no commercial relationship with OpenAI.

The data captures the last click before each visit, but it doesn’t include prompts, ad impressions, or users’ subscription tiers. For the paid side, advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, so this comparison reflects their results rather than proving the ads caused them.

You can calculate the parity price for your own account by dividing the revenue per visit from ChatGPT ads by the revenue per visit from paid search, then multiplying the result by your search cost per click. The result is the price at which ChatGPT clicks would match search on tracked revenue per dollar. It leaves out profit margins and any later purchases the last click doesn’t capture.

Before you compare, make sure to check your ChatGPT ad sessions for ad review crawler visits. According to OpenAI’s basics page, it is possible for crawlers of this type (ad-review) to visit landing pages using tracking parameters, and third-party analytics tools can flag these types of visits as paid. Other reported results are more favorable, though they were based upon different metrics than those used by the authors of the paper. On Aug. 31, OpenAI posted that an ecommerce advertiser experienced a return on ad spend of three times their investment over a period of 28 days. Additionally, according to DoubleVerify, the attributed cost per acquisition for Weight Watchers was 15.3% less than their benchmark.

The paper’s data ends Aug. 22. OpenAI has since expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries and says more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns. Its Aug. 31 post said CPC and outcome-optimized bidding accounted for most campaigns.

The authors are suggesting that since ad clicks for ChatGPT appear as sponsored cards and therefore appear separately from the answer, they could be worth little. On top of this, if OpenAI were to move the ads in with the answer (i.e. remove the separation) the value of an ad click could go up but at the same time so could the number of people who distrust ChatGPT’s answers. OpenAI’s Oct. 21 post says its ads are labeled and kept apart from answers. The same post says the company is “continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.”

#7593. Do videos with excessive motion help kids pay attention, or are they just distractions?

A recent study looked into a rising trend in children’s content — and the results suggest that educators should proceed with caution. Researchers at the Indian School of Business and Santa Clara University tracked eye movements on educational videos with moving backgrounds and found that those videos both command attention and deflect it onto the noisy backgrounds.

The study spanned more than 32,000 videos that were tagged as being “made for kids.” The researchers tracked the eye movements of kids between the ages of six and ten and noted the view rates for those clips. Then, background motion was added to those videos, and viewing habits were measured again.

While a wide range of videos were included in the study, the idea of an educational video with unrelated background motion conjures up images of some specific content formats. Perhaps you’ve seen them: They’re videos that pair dense explanations with overlaid footage of oddly satisfying compilations or Minecraft gameplay sessions.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Thanks to so-called “pdf-to-brainrot” generators, those mash-ups have become study aids for some students. They’ve even made it into the realm of politics. In 2024, for example, the Kamala Harris campaign paired World of Warcraft gameplay with a Tim Walz rally.

Clearly, the adults using this split-screen approach believe it keeps eyes glued to the screen, even among viewers with short attention spans. According to the recent study, that idea is only half true. The researchers found that videos with “high motion” had 2% higher view rates compared to more inert content. But those viewers weren’t necessarily keeping their attention on the educational parts of those videos. Instead, the researchers noted that their subjects’ eyes would follow the moving backgrounds rather than the didactic foregrounds.

Distracting as these videos may be, they can serve a beneficial purpose. The researchers suggested that educators should apply the results to harness the attention-grabbing nature of moving backgrounds.

“Motion is a powerful design lever, but it must be used intentionally,” said Madhu Viswanathan, an Associate Professor of Marketing at the Indian School of Business. “Rather than maximizing continuous stimulation throughout a video, creators should use targeted motion to facilitate attention recovery during moments where attention drift is most expected.”

Several apps have already committed to the “TikTokification” of contemporary education. Revyze and ScrollEd are two platforms that try to keep kids focused by presenting them with kinetic learning environments. The popularity of those apps shows that the concept of fast-paced educational videos is catching on with students, but the recent research shows that a methodical approach will be important if students’ scrolling behaviors is to translate to positive learning outcomes.

#7591. ZoomInfo Technologies LLC: Principal Applied AI Engineer - Entity Agents

ZoomInfo is where careers accelerate. We move fast, think boldly, and empower you to do the best work of your life. You’ll be surrounded by teammates who care deeply, challenge each other, and celebrate wins. With tools that amplify your impact and a culture that backs your ambition, you won’t just contribute. You’ll make things happen fast.

ZoomInfo is where careers accelerate. We move fast, think boldly, and empower you to do the best work of your life. You’ll be surrounded by teammates who care deeply, challenge each other, and celebrate wins. With tools that amplify your impact and a culture that backs your ambition, you won’t just contribute, you’ll make things happen, fast.

ZoomInfo’s Core Data team builds the company and contact data behind the Go-To-Market Intelligence Platform: hundreds of millions of records, resolved to the right entity, kept accurate, and delivered to more than 35,000 customers.

The way that data is produced is changing. For years it came from deterministic pipelines: many sources, weighted and decayed, one winner per attribute. Core Data is now moving to AI-native data management, where an agent pursues the evidence for an entity, decides every attribute over all of it, and records why. The company and contact agents already exist as working, measured prototypes. What does not exist yet is the machinery that runs them at production volume, proves every version before it ships, and lets researchers and product managers operate them without an engineer in the loop.

We are hiring a Senior Applied AI Engineer to build and own that machinery. You will complete the entity-agent pipeline, build the evidence adapters behind a single envelope, run the benchmark and golden-gate system on a schedule, build the review and batch tooling the team operates, and carry the agents onto ZoomInfo’s Agentic Platform. You will work with the Principal AI Engineer who owns the benchmark harness and productionization, the product manager who owns evaluation and policy, and the company and person engineering teams that own the pipelines the agents feed. You will not be the only person who can do this work; you will be the second, so that neither of you is a single point of failure.

This is a role for someone who has shipped LLM systems in production with evaluations, builds platform for other people to operate, and can work inside a large-scale data pipeline. You should be as comfortable writing an adapter with a replayable store and a kill switch as you are reading a miss analysis with a product manager, and you should like that the prototype you take to production was built by a PM who commits code.

Run the benchmark and golden-gate system. Move judge runs, golden-gate results, arms scorecards, and cost per record from a laptop to a scheduled system against staging. Every agent version is gated automatically, with variance and drift tracked per release. The evaluation product manager sets the thresholds; you make them enforceable.

Complete the entity-agent pipeline. Build the stages that do not exist yet: enricher fan-out, location sets, and hierarchy batch files. Migrate the classifiers to the shared runner with the Principal AI Engineer so they run at production scale. Measure throughput and unit cost per stage on named cohorts, so the cost model comes from instrumentation rather than estimates.

Build the evidence adapters. Registries, live web, mail-tenant signals, and external research vendors all sit behind one envelope with a replayable vendor store, measured lift per shape, a per-vendor kill switch, and at least two sources per shape. Vendors are swappable by design.

Deploy onto the ZoomInfo Agentic Platform. Carry the company and contact agents through the production plan onto ZAP, build the ingest adapter side (envelope to match service and bulk intake), and keep a rollback path per version. Keep the DOH implementation and the platform implementation upgraded in lockstep, enforced by tooling.

Make the loop self-service. Build the review queue, tagging tools, blast-radius viewer, and batch runners that researchers and product managers use without an engineer. Measure review yield and golden-record production.

Keep the agent surfaces alive. Own the health and deployment of the company classifier, contact classifier, agents hub, and judge platform inside our internal tooling, so the team’s iteration cycle never waits on one person.

Instrument everything. Cost per call, per row, per stage; quality per version; alerts before a human notices.

A builder who ships. You pick the boring technology when it wins and you would rather have a running adapter than a design doc.

An evaluator by instinct. You do not release a version without a test set, a threshold, and a number for what it costs.

A platform thinker. You build things that other people run, and you design for the day the vendor goes down.

Comfortable in the data. You can read a pipeline, reason about matching, and explain why a wrong merge is worse than a missed one.

Tenacious. ZoomInfo is fast, distributed, and messy. You go find the people you need and drive the work to done.

One team. Honest, has the team’s back, celebrates wins and losses together.

You report to the Senior Manager of Product for Core Data, with the Principal AI Engineer as your technical lead, and sit inside the Core and Global Data organization under the Chief Data Officer. Your day-to-day partners are the Principal AI Engineer, the product manager who owns evaluation and data policy, the Company and Person Data product managers, the research team that grades and rules, the agentic platform team, and company and person engineering. Expect interesting problems: how do you run a judge over a million records a day for cents, not dollars? How do you make a vendor replaceable without a rewrite? How do you let a researcher run a batch and rule on the misses without paging you?

#7588. Druski is one of Netflix’s biggest creator signings. What can he do with a multi-year deal?

Druski is coming to Netflix. On December 1, the ascendant creator (whose real name is Drew Desbordes) will premiere Collect & Praise, a comedy series that spoofs the culture of megachurches.

Since making a name for himself with Instagram Live broadcasts and short-form sketches, Druski has become a bankable star. He has appeared in campaigns alongside traditional celebs, spun podcast gold, and even launched his own agency.

His fame will reach new heights (and new audiences) on November 7. That’s when he will become the first social media creator to host Saturday Night Live.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Druski leveraged his expanding network to make Collect & Praise a reality. The self-funded series, produced through his company 4LIFERS Entertainment, builds on viral sketches he has posted and co-stars veteran comic actor Mike Epps. On the Diary of a CEO podcast, Druski told Steven Bartlett that his show triggered a “bidding war,” with Netflifx coming out on top.

As we’ve seen with the streaming platform’s other creator deals, its agreement with Druski will go beyond original content. Netflix will license content from the creator’s back catalog, including his dating show parody Coulda Been Love and his semi-serious label Coulda Been Records.

“I’ve built my platform by creating characters and comedy that resonate with people,” Druski said in a statement. “This partnership with Netflix will give me the resources to build on that comedy foundation and bring my work to a new global audience. It’s a tremendous opportunity for our team at 4LIFERS Entertainment to expand our reach, develop original programming for the masses and take our creativity to new heights.”

A multi-year agreement will give Druski plenty of time to flex his creative muscles. Netflix’s press release promises “future Druski projects” on the platform; those ventures will be announced at a later date.

Netflix certainly hasn’t been shy about signing creators. It has inked deals with Mark Rober, Alan Chikin Chow, and several other digital standouts as it looks to encroach on YouTube’s territory.

That spending spree, however, hasn’t been able to abate the negative headlines at Netflix HQ. A big round of layoffs hit last month, and erratic earnings have sent the streamer’s stock price tumbling. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos, normally an optimist about his company’s outlook, has admitted that Netflix “could do better.”

Perhaps Druski’s star power will be the shot in the arm Netflix needs to set itself on an upward course. If, however, Collect & Praise doesn’t pan out as expected, Netflix may be left wondering what coulda been.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.
